Key Research Thinking Patterns: Multiscale Urban Thermal Driver Analysis: Utilizing Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) on global TCI datasets to quantify the spatial heterogeneity of thermal stress, revealing that topographic and socioeconomic factors often outweigh vegetation in regulating urban heat.

Explainable Machine Learning for Urban Form Optimization: Integrating XGBoost with SHAP values to identify non-linear thresholds and seasonal variations in Land Surface Temperature (LST) responses to built-up indices (NDBI) and vegetation diversity (SHDI) at block and grid scales.

Landscape Ecology-Driven Cooling Strategy: Applying Local Climate Zone (LCZ) classification combined with landscape pattern indices (LSI, PLAND, COHESION) to determine how internal and surrounding greenspace configurations differentially impact daytime cooling in compact versus open building zones.

High-Resolution Remote Sensing for Precision Monitoring: Developing algorithmic methods like STEM-OP for single-tree extraction in agriculture and employing Random Forest downscaling of Landsat data to correct biases in urban park cooling effect assessments, ensuring accurate heat governance metrics.
Summary Description: Xiangming Xiao specializes in urban climatology and remote sensing, focusing on mitigating urban heat islands through advanced geospatial analysis. By integrating machine learning (XGBoost, SHAP) with landscape ecology metrics, the researcher quantifies the complex, non-linear relationships between urban form, greenspace configuration, and Land Surface Temperature (LST) across global and local scales. Key contributions include identifying the superior role of topography over vegetation in global heat stress, optimizing urban park cooling assessments via high-resolution data downscaling, and developing precise monitoring tools for agricultural systems. This work provides critical, data-driven insights for climate-resilient urban planning and sustainable environmental management.
